Modern subjects in traditional artistic languages.  

Prompt: Translate exterior maintenance on a modern space station into a Tang-dynasty Dunhuang-style earthen-wall mural in rich mineral pigments. The image is a flat wall painting, not a space movie. At the center, a technician resembling a flying apsara reaches sideways toward a solar-panel pivot, wearing a simplified modern safety vest over wide sleeves, with long ribbons forming two flowing arcs behind them. A companion at the lower left passes a tool to the main figure, while another at the upper right steadies a folded solar panel. All three direct their hands and eyes toward the same pivot. Clear, fine safety lines connect the figures to the station wall; ribbons and safety tethers each follow distinct paths and must not merge into tangled lines. The station consists of an ocher-white cylinder and a few geometric planes, with solar panels rendered as small azurite-blue squares. Make the modern facilities recognizable without smooth metal or realistic space lighting. Use Tang-mural-style linework for faces and clothing folds, light bodily contours, and overlapping forms instead of precise perspective. Render Earth at the side as a muted malachite-green disc. Keep the background earthen ocher with a few traditional scrolling clouds and star dots. Balance cinnabar red, azurite blue, malachite green, and warm white. Show mineral grains and slight natural wear in the paint layers, with locally exposed wall substrate rather than a uniform crackle filter. Organize movement through ribbons, panel wings, and the cylinder. Make the main figure large and the helpers slightly smaller, leaving open wall areas that breathe like blank paper. No sci-fi armor, blue volumetric light, photographic starfields, subtitles, trademarks, inscriptions, or seals.

16 reference images in a single generation.

tweets.text:
"Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL"

Training AI models to detect and penalize cheating can actually teach them to become better at hiding it, as models learn to exploit weaknesses in their monitors rather than stop reward hacking.

So this paper investigate how to design more effective monitors during RL training, because they found that the monitor robustness matters more than initial accuracy. This includes stronger judges and carefully balanced penalties.

Across benchmarks, their improved interventions reduce reward hacking by 23.2% in medical chat and 86.2% in biography generation, with the latter pretty eliminating the behavior in their experiments.

https://t.co/T69lLaBHZA

We replicated all 9 experiments from the original weight-space programming blog.

Some interesting findings:

- Experiment 4 (Repair a car policy): Our one-shot edit took the car from 0/1,024 to 1,024/1,024 ramp climbs while editing just 4,813 weights, 21% fewer than the authors
- Experiment 5 (Writing video game policies from scratch): With all weights initialized to 0, GPT-6 Astra wrote a policy for Breakout that scored 309.9 on average, around ~12x higher than the blog
- Experiment 8 (Editing Qwen3.5-0.8B for math): While the authors got to 48.1% on MATH-500 with 50 passes, we could only achieve 34.4%.

We’ve made this a publicly available project where you can see the full agent traces, view experimental artifacts like activations from sample forward passes, ask follow-up questions, and even continue experimenting.

Check out the project at: https://t.co/ymcjTj6EzC

AI coding agents could bring the next paradigm shift in robotics by learning to control robots through code.

With that in mind, this paper introduces Embodied First Exam, the first robotics benchmark with 1,156 tasks across 47 robots, testing whether coding agents can directly control robots, write controllers, or train their own policies under different physical-world constraints.

And the results also show how far we still have to go. On 391 matched tasks, the strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra, achieves 77% success with full simulator access and unlimited resets, but only 30% under more realistic constraints. 

In real-time evaluations, 63% of tasks remain unsolved by any of the 8 agents tested.

https://t.co/e6dL1VUFTa

x.name: Dan Shipper
x.bio: ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI

tweets.text:
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:
this week @every https://t.co/IqurhRhS5w

x.name: Aditya Agarwal
x.bio: General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early Eng @facebook, CTO @Dropbox, Board @Flipkart | Optimist, Builder, Dad

tweets.text:
It has been such a pleasure to partner with Rox from the earliest days.

I have also learnt a lot about what it means to run a company at AI-pace from @ishanmkh. His talk at our recent founder retreat was incredible. https://t.co/UdZlqzZetx

There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now.

1. Diffusion of AI
This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done.

Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here.

2. Frontier of AI
This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress.

It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc:

- Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you.

- Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease.

- VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms.

- Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry.

(There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.)

Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.
